note: Starting points, not an inventory. Every organisation is different: take what fits, change the wording, and delete the rest. Scores are a first guess to argue with, not an answer. The outcomes shown against each risk are the subcategories it belongs to.

items.name: Key personnel / single points of knowledge

items.title: Unpatched critical vulnerability exploited
items.description: A known flaw in an internet-facing system is not patched in time and is exploited before anyone notices it was outstanding.

items.title: Staff credentials taken by phishing
items.description: An employee enters their password and one-time code on a convincing fake sign-in page, handing an attacker a working session.

items.title: Ransomware encrypts servers and backups
items.description: Ransomware spreads to file servers and reaches the backups as well, so recovery takes weeks instead of hours.

items.title: Supplier breach exposes your information
items.description: A supplier holding or processing your data is compromised, and your customers are affected by an incident that never touched your network.

items.title: Cloud storage or service left publicly accessible
items.description: A misconfiguration exposes a storage bucket, database or admin console to the internet, usually discovered by somebody outside the organisation.

items.title: Privileged administrator misuses their access
items.description: Someone with unrestricted rights reads, changes or deletes what they should not, and without logging nobody can prove what happened.

items.title: Leaver keeps access after departure
items.description: Accounts and equipment are not taken back when someone leaves, so a former employee or contractor still has a working way in.

items.title: Malware spreads across a flat network
items.description: An infection on one laptop reaches servers and other offices because the network is not divided, turning one machine into an organisation-wide incident.

items.title: Vulnerable third-party library shipped to production
items.description: An open-source component with a known flaw is built into an application because nothing checks what the software is made of.

items.title: Sensitive data leaves by email or removable media
items.description: A member of staff sends or copies confidential information out of the organisation, whether by mistake or on purpose.

items.title: Intrusion goes undetected for months
items.description: An attacker is inside the network but nothing raises an alarm, and logs from different systems cannot be lined up to work out what happened.

items.title: Recovery fails when it is actually needed
items.description: Recovery plans exist on paper but have never been tested, and the systems do not come back when the main site or cloud region is lost.

items.title: Expired certificate takes a service down
items.description: Nobody owns a certificate or is warned before it lapses, and a public service stops working for reasons that look like an attack.

items.title: Untested change breaks production
items.description: A change is made straight in the live environment without testing or a way back, causing an outage. More outages come from changes than from attackers.

items.title: Systems in use that nobody knows about
items.description: Teams buy or build their own tools, so information sits outside every control the organisation believes it has.

items.title: Information security has no clear owner or backing
items.description: Responsibility is spread across roles with nobody accountable and no support from management, so nothing improves between audits.

items.title: Incident handled badly because nobody knows the plan
items.description: When something goes wrong, people do not know who to call or what to do first, so the damage grows while roles are argued over.

items.title: Breach not reported to authorities in time
items.description: A personal data breach is not recognised or escalated quickly enough, and the deadline to tell the regulator or the people affected is missed.

items.title: Evidence destroyed while responding to an incident
items.description: In the rush to restore service, logs are overwritten and machines rebuilt, so the cause cannot be proved and legal action or an insurance claim fails.

items.title: The same incident keeps happening
items.description: Incidents are closed as soon as service is back, nobody looks for the cause, and the same weakness is exploited again months later.

items.title: Laptop lost or stolen with unencrypted data
items.description: A laptop or phone is left on a train or taken from a car, and the information on it is readable by whoever has it.

items.title: Home working exposes confidential information
items.description: People work from home or in public places on shared devices and open screens, with papers left out and conversations overheard.

items.title: Person hired on false credentials given access
items.description: Someone joins with a faked history or undisclosed conflicts, and receives access to sensitive information before any checks are done.

items.title: Staff mishandle information because nothing says how sensitive it is
items.description: Documents and data carry no classification or label, so confidential material is shared, printed and stored like everything else.

items.title: Staff ignore security rules because nothing happens when they do
items.description: Rules are published but breaking them has no consequence, so shortcuts become normal practice and the policy is ignored.

items.title: Unauthorised person gets into the office or server room
items.description: Someone gets in by following staff through a door, using an old badge or walking in unescorted, and reaches equipment or papers.

items.title: Fire, flood or power loss in the server room
items.description: Equipment in a poorly protected room is damaged by water, heat or an electrical fault, or stops when the power fails.

items.title: Equipment or cabling fails for lack of care
items.description: Unmaintained equipment breaks down and exposed cabling is damaged or tapped, taking systems down without warning.

items.title: Old equipment disposed of with data still on it
items.description: Laptops, disks and phones are sold, recycled or thrown away without being wiped, and the information on them is recovered by someone else.

items.title: Real customer data exposed in test environments
items.description: Copies of live data are used for development and testing, where access is loose and nobody treats it as sensitive.

items.title: Source code or secrets stolen from the repository
items.description: Source code, passwords or keys in a code repository are copied by someone who should not have access, exposing products and systems.

items.title: An audit or test disrupts live systems
items.description: A vulnerability scan, penetration test or audit query runs against production without planning, and slows or stops a live service.

items.title: Unlicensed software or copied material in use
items.description: Software, fonts, images or documents are used without the right licence, leading to fines, legal claims or forced removal.

items.title: Warnings about new threats not acted on
items.description: Alerts from suppliers, industry groups or authorities about an active threat arrive, but nobody reads them or checks whether they apply.

items.title: Security left out of new projects
items.description: Projects and new systems are designed and bought without security requirements, so weaknesses are built in and costly to fix later.

items.title: Systems run out of capacity at peak times
items.description: Storage, processing or network capacity is not watched, and a service slows or fails at the busiest moment.

items.title: Controls exist on paper but nobody checks they work
items.description: Policies and procedures are written but never independently reviewed, so gaps are only found by an external auditor or an attacker.

items.title: Key tasks only one person knows how to do
items.description: Backups, restores and admin tasks are done from memory by one person, and nobody else can do them when that person is away or leaves.

items.title: Access granted without approval and never reviewed
items.description: People collect access as they move between roles because requests are not approved and nobody reviews who has what.

items.title: Weak or shared passwords
items.description: Shared accounts, default passwords and simple passwords reused across systems let one leaked password open many doors.

items.title: Legal or contractual requirement missed
items.description: A law, regulation or customer contract sets a security or privacy obligation that nobody has listed, and it is breached without anyone knowing.

items.title: Records lost or destroyed too early
items.description: Records that must be kept for legal or business reasons are deleted, damaged or cannot be found when a regulator or court asks for them.

items.title: Supplier changes its service without telling you
items.description: A cloud or managed service provider changes how its service works, where data is held or who subcontracts it, and nobody reviews the effect.

items.title: Harmful websites and downloads reach staff
items.description: Staff browse to malicious or compromised websites and download infected files, because nothing filters where they can go.

items.title: Nobody has said what the organisation is for, so security guesses
items.description: Security decisions are made without an agreed view of the mission, the services that matter most, or what the organisation depends on, so effort goes to the wrong places.

items.title: No agreed risk appetite, so every decision is argued from scratch
items.description: There is no statement of how much risk is acceptable, so each decision is relitigated and inconsistent, and nobody can say whether a given exposure is tolerable.

items.title: Risk is scored differently by everyone who scores it
items.description: Without one method for calculating and recording risk, two teams rate the same exposure differently and the register cannot be ranked or trusted.

items.title: Bad news does not travel upwards
items.description: Lines of communication for risk are unclear, so problems are known at the working level months before anyone who could fund a fix hears about them.

items.title: An opportunity to reduce risk cheaply is missed
items.description: A change that would have improved security while saving money - a platform migration, a retirement, a contract renewal - passes without anybody considering it.

items.title: No security policy, or one nobody has revisited
items.description: There is no approved policy setting expectations, or it was written years ago and no longer matches how the organisation works.

items.title: Suppliers are managed by contract alone
items.description: There is no supply chain programme: suppliers are not prioritised by criticality, security requirements are not agreed before signing, and nobody checks afterwards.

items.title: A critical supplier is chosen without any assessment
items.description: A supplier handling important data or services is engaged with no security due diligence, and the risk is discovered after the contract is signed.

items.title: A supplier is left out of the incident plan
items.description: When something goes wrong at a supplier, nobody knows who to call, what they owe you, or how the two incident processes fit together.

items.title: A supplier relationship ends badly
items.description: A contract ends or a supplier fails, and data, access and obligations are not wound down: accounts stay open and information stays where it was.

items.title: Supply chain risk sits outside the risk process
items.description: Supplier risks are tracked in a spreadsheet by procurement and never reach the register that leadership reviews.

items.title: Nobody reviews whether the strategy is working
items.description: Objectives and performance are never evaluated, so the programme continues unchanged whether it is succeeding or not.

items.title: Risk decisions are made and then forgotten
items.description: Responses are agreed but not prioritised, planned or tracked, so the same risks appear at the next review in the same state.

items.title: Specialists are given no training for their role
items.description: People in security, development and administration roles get the same general awareness session as everybody else, and nothing about the work they actually do.

items.title: Events are noticed but never sized
items.description: Alerts are seen and closed without working out how far the problem reached, so incidents are declared late or not at all.

items.title: The people who need to know are not told
items.description: Adverse events are handled quietly by the technical team; the staff who could act on them, and the stakeholders who should hear, are not informed.

items.title: Reports pile up without triage
items.description: Suspected incidents are reported but not validated or ranked, so a serious one waits behind a queue of false alarms.

items.title: Recovery drags on with no end in sight
items.description: There is no criterion for declaring recovery complete, so systems are restored piecemeal, stakeholders are not updated, and the incident never formally closes.

items.title: Restored systems are trusted without being checked
items.description: Services are brought back from backup and declared healthy without verifying their integrity, so a compromise or corruption comes back with them.

items.title: Data the business depends on is not identified
items.description: Nobody has listed the important data and where it lives, so protection is applied to systems rather than to what matters inside them.

items.title: Nation-State Targeted Intrusion
items.description: A state-sponsored threat actor conducts a sustained campaign against government systems to steal sensitive information or disrupt services.

items.title: Large-Scale Citizen Data Registry Breach
items.description: A breach of a citizen records system exposes personal data for a large portion of the population, triggering mass notification obligations.

items.title: Leakage of Classified or Sensitive Information
items.description: An insider or mishandling incident results in classified or sensitive government information being disclosed outside authorized channels.

items.title: Disruption of Critical Public Services
items.description: An attack or system failure disrupts a critical public service (e.g. benefits, permits, emergency systems), affecting citizens directly.

items.title: Legacy Systems Supporting Essential Services
items.description: Core government services run on ageing, unsupported systems that are increasingly difficult to secure or maintain.

items.title: Uncontrolled Cross-Agency Data Sharing
items.description: Citizen data is shared between agencies without consistent controls, increasing the risk of misuse or unauthorized secondary use.

items.title: Excessive Contractor Access to Sensitive Systems
items.description: External contractors retain broad access to sensitive government systems beyond what their engagement requires.

items.title: Website Defacement or Disinformation
items.description: A public-facing government website is defaced or used to spread disinformation, damaging public trust in official communications.

items.title: Records Management and Freedom-of-Information Failures
items.description: Poor records management results in the organisation being unable to meet statutory records-retention or freedom-of-information obligations.

items.title: Procurement Fraud via System Manipulation
items.description: Procurement or payment systems are manipulated to divert public funds to fraudulent suppliers.

items.title: Unauthorized Staff Lookups of Citizen Records
items.description: Government employees access citizen records out of curiosity or for personal reasons without a legitimate case-related need, breaching citizens' privacy.
